title: Islanded Hot-Pool Strategy, Tenant Credit Ledger & Eviction Playbook
content:
Purpose:
This draft proposes an 'islanded hot-pool' approach for handling short-duration burst demand on Dedicated capacity that preserves tenant isolation, offers a transparent credit-based burst model, and provides a deterministic eviction/playbook mechanism when oversubscription occurs. The goal is to let teams run spiky workloads with predictable SLO outcomes and clear cost/chargeback semantics while avoiding noisy-neighbor incidents that jeopardize committed SLAs.

Scope:
- Applies to Dedicated GPU pools (reserved capacity) only.
- Covers control-plane rules for: hot-pool sizing, tenant credit issuance/decay, soft-preemption profiles, eviction ordering, and observability signals for billing & SLOs.
- Does NOT cover on-prem physical provisioning or non-GPU accelerators in this draft.

Background / Problem Statement:
Teams with reserved Dedicated capacity frequently need occasional short bursts (seconds to a few minutes) of additional tokens to handle sudden traffic spikes (batch generation, internal retrain jobs, or marketing bursts). Current options: permanent over-provisioning or immediate hard-eviction when pool limits reached. Both are costly or brittle. We need a semi-opportunistic mechanism to serve bursts with:
- predictability for committed tenants,
- fair allocation so smaller tenants do not get starved,
- clear charging and operational triggers.

Design Goals:
1) Preserve SLOs for committed lanes (latency guarantees) even under burst conditions.
2) Offer controlled short-term access to unused capacity via an islanded hot-pool abstraction.
3) Make burst consumption auditable and billable (credit ledger).
4) Provide deterministic, low-noise eviction and fallback behavior when hot capacity is exhausted.
5) Minimize operator intervention; prefer automated safe rollbacks.

Overview of the Proposal:
- Islanded Hot-Pool: a transient, soft-isolated set of GPU slots carved from fraction of Dedicated cluster capacity (configurable per zone/cluster). It accepts burst allocations but is constrained by per-tenant credit and global headroom limits.
- Tenant Burst Credit Ledger: every tenant has a ledger of burst credits. Credits are earned by commit level, historical utilization smoothing, or purchased. Credits decay on a predictable schedule to avoid unbounded credit accumulation.
- Soft Preemption Profiles: requests served out of hot-pool can be marked as preemptible with one of several profiles (gentle, immediate, graceful). These profiles determine how the runtime degrades the request (queue, slowdown, response stub, or immediate fallback to committed model).
- Eviction Playbook: deterministic ordering for preemption based on credit balance, tenant tier, and active SLO weight. Includes operator-facing runbook and automated fallback.

Key Concepts and Rules:
1) Hot-Pool Allocation and Sizing:
   - Default hot-pool size: 5% of cluster GPU slots, configurable per Dedicated cluster.
   - Hot-pool has a minimum guaranteed isolation from committed pools; it cannot reduce headroom for committed lanes below the configured safety buffer.
   - A cluster-level utility meter tracks hot-pool fill, burst acceptance rate, and average burst duration.

2) Tenant Burst Credits:
   - Ledger fields (logical only): balance, accrual_rate, max_balance, decay_half_life_seconds, last_update_timestamp.
   - Earning rules: free baseline earned daily for committed customers; additional allocation given on annual or contractual commitment; ad-hoc purchase via credits pack.
   - Consumption: credits consumed proportionally to GPU-seconds used and the model-fidelity multiplier (bigger models cost more credits per second).
   - Decay: credits decay with half-life (configurable per account) to prevent hoarding and align economics.

3) Request Classification:
   - Requests tagged as HOT_BURST, HOT_PREFETCH, or NORMAL. SDK/API accepts burst hint boolean and expected duration percentile.
   - Control-plane checks: if tenant credit >= estimated cost and hot-pool headroom >= estimated slot, accept into hot-pool. Otherwise, route to queue, deny, or fall back.

4) Soft Preemption Profiles (examples):
   - Gentle: allow request to run; if preempted, keep partial output cached and resume on fallback model; preserve tokens where possible; 30s graceful window.
   - Graceful: complete sub-second checkpoints and return partial response with status=degraded; 10s window.
   - Immediate: instant evict and return 429/fallback; intended for best-effort workloads.

5) Eviction and Fairness Ordering:
When global headroom is exhausted, eviction occurs with this order:
   a) Hot-pool requests with Immediate profile and zero credits.
   b) Hot-pool requests sorted by (credit_balance / committed_commitment_weight) ascending.
   c) Cross-check against tenant safety list: emergency-flagged tenants are protected and will be skipped (requires compliance approval).
   d) Tie-breaker: least-recently-used by active burst start time.
This ordering balances contractual priority and credit fairness while making evictions predictable.

6) Billing and Chargeback:
   - Credits consumption is logged per request. A daily reconciliation job emits CSV exports for invoicing.
   - Overdraft allowed with penalty multiplier for enterprise customers (configurable). Overdrafts generate alerts to customer billing contacts.

7) Observability and Alerts:
   - Per-tenant dashboards: credit balance, burn-rate, hot-pool acceptance rate, eviction count, fallback percent.
   - Cluster-level metrics: hot-pool occupancy, average burst duration, preemption events per minute, SLO violation delta for committed lanes.
   - Alerting: when hot-pool acceptance > threshold for > n minutes, paging to ops and notifying affected tenants with suggested mitigations.

8) APIs and UX:
   - Admin API to set tenant ledger parameters (accrual, max_balance, decay).
   - Public request hinting fields in Redwood SDK: { burst_hint: true, expected_p95_duration_ms: 1000, preemption_profile: "gentle" }.
   - Console: line-item for consumed burst credits and projected burn for next 24h.

Operational Runbook (high-level):
- Detection:
  1) Pager triggers when cluster hot-pool rejection ratio > 20% for 3m AND committed-lane latency regresses > SLA delta.
- Immediate mitigation:
  1) Temporarily reduce hot-pool max to 0% in the affected cluster (fails open to queued fallback).
  2) Trigger automated fallback policy to nearest compatible model in hosted/dedicated if allowed.
  3) Notify top-3 burst consumers via configured contacts to throttle.
- Post-incident:
  1) Reconcile ledger CSVs and check for incorrect credit charging.
  2) Run failure simulation to validate eviction ordering.
  3) Draft postmortem with action items: tuning decay_half_life, adjusting default hot-pool percent, or adding capacity.

SLOs and Safety Targets:
- Committed-lane latency SLO must not exceed baseline by more than 10% during normal hot-pool operation.
- Hot-pool preemption should occur without impacting committed-lane availability; design target: < 1 minute to throttle and < 5% SLO violations attributable to hot-pool events.

Rollout Plan:
1) Lab prototype in a single non-prod cluster with synthetic burst workload.
2) Canary in 2 small Dedicated clusters with subset of tenants opted-in (beta).
3) Expand to 20% of clusters and expose purchase/credit UI.
4) Full launch with tenant-facing SLAs and billing integration.

Risks and Mitigations:
- Risk: Misconfigured accruals let tenants use disproportionate hot capacity.
  Mitigation: default caps, automated anomaly detectors, quota alerts.
- Risk: Confusing UX around credits leading to surprise invoices.
  Mitigation: pre-burn warnings, projected cost UI, free baseline.
- Risk: Preemption causing unacceptable model quality regressions.
  Mitigation: restrict immediate profile for production-critical models; add qa-eval-based gating.

Open Questions / Discussion Items:
- Should we expose a purely time-based non-credit burst (free for low-severity bursts) for small tenants?
- What should be default hot-pool percent for on-prem Dedicated deployments? (5% vs 10%)
- How to tie credit pricing to model class more granularly (per-param or per-flop)?

Next Steps / Action Items:
- Engineering: prototype credit ledger shim and request-side tagging (JIRA-DED-4557) - owner: Omar.
- Infra: add hot-pool telemetry metrics (github PR referenced). - owner: Leo.
- Product: design credit purchase UX and console placement (mockups due 2025-03-15) - owner: Priya.
- Legal/Billing: map credit events to invoice lines for accounting - owner: Sophie.

Appendix A — Example Scenarios:
1) Marketing spike: Tenant A buys a 1-hour credit pack. They burst for 12m, consume credits, no impact to tenant B committed lane. Post-burst, ledger decays slightly over 24h.
2) Fleet-wide holiday surge: hot-pool exhausted; eviction ordering removes several immediate-profile batch jobs from lower-tier tenants, committed lanes remain within SLO. Billing generates overdraft alerts.

Appendix B — Minimal Data Model (logical) for ledger (for engineering intake):
- tenant_id (string)
- balance (float credits)
- accrual_rate (credits/day)
- decay_half_life_seconds (int)
- max_balance (float)
- reserved_flag (bool)
- last_update_iso (timestamp)

Note: Above is logical only — keep persisted schema in infra PR.

Contact / Owners:
- Product owner: Maya Chen (mchen@redwood.com)
- Engineering lead: Omar Rodriguez (orodriguez@redwood.com)

This is a working draft — expect iterations. Primary feedback requested: fairness formula for eviction ordering, default hot-pool percent, and suggested preemption profile semantics.
